028998ee-babc-4096-9b28-001bc2f9a84e.summary:
Tomos Ellis, a 15-year-old male with no documented past medical history, medications, or allergies, presented via A&E on 07/01/2026 at 08:45 with 3 days of worsening constant lower abdominal pain and constipation. He reported reduced appetite and mild nausea without vomiting or fever. Examination showed mild abdominal distension and lower-quadrant tenderness without guarding, rebound tenderness, or peritonism. Mild dehydration was noted, with slightly dry mucous membranes and reduced skin turgor; observations were stable.

He was initially diagnosed with constipation. He was kept NPO/NBM and commenced on 0.9% sodium chloride IV fluids, 500 mL over 4 hours. Blood tests, including FBC, U&Es, CRP, and LFTs, were normal. Abdominal X-ray demonstrated significant faecal loading without obstruction or perforation. A single 10 mg oral dose of bisacodyl was given, and he was admitted to the paediatric ward for supportive management and observation.

On medical review, abdominal pain had reduced from approximately 6–7/10 to 5/10 following IV fluids. Oral macrogol (Movicol) was commenced, initially documented as one sachet three times daily, with encouragement of oral hydration and monitoring of bowel movements and symptoms. A subsequent ward round plan documented macrogol one sachet twice daily and a target fluid intake of at least 2 L/day. He received advice regarding dietary fibre and hydration, with written information provided to him and his mother. Physiotherapy sessions on 07/01 and 08/01 focused on gentle mobilisation, stretching, and walking to promote bowel motility; these were well tolerated. A dietitian recommended a high-fibre diet including whole grains, fruit, and vegetables.

By the following ward review, he had passed a partial bowel movement overnight, with reduced abdominal pain and less distension. Macrogol was continued at one sachet three times daily, with ongoing hydration advice. On the subsequent review, he had passed a full bowel movement overnight, with complete resolution of abdominal pain. He was comfortable, hydrated, and had a soft, non-tender abdomen without guarding or rebound tenderness; observations remained stable.

Macrogol was discontinued. He was discharged with lactulose 10 mL twice daily as required for maintenance, advice to maintain oral hydration and a high-fibre diet, and recommendations for gentle walking at home. His GP was informed of the admission, treatment, and discharge plan, and the patient and family were advised to contact the GP if constipation recurred.

04df53ea-55c1-48d9-84a1-1f15c133b29b.summary:
67-year-old man with hypertension and osteoarthritis, taking no regular medications and with no known drug allergies, presented on 01/01/2026 after a minor fall with acute confusion and disorientation to time and place. Initial observations included BP 170/95, HR 88 and GCS 12/15, improving to 13–14/15 during assessment. He reported no loss of consciousness, vomiting, visual symptoms, seizures, or focal neurological symptoms; a mild occipital headache was documented by the neurology team. Examination showed no external trauma or focal neurological deficit.

Initial CT head demonstrated a subdural hygroma without midline shift or acute haemorrhage. FBC, urea and electrolytes, and coagulation studies were initially reported as normal, although mild hyponatraemia (Na 132 mmol/L) was subsequently identified and considered contributory to the confusion. He was admitted to the Neurology Ward for four-hourly neurological observations, mobilisation as tolerated, and repeat CT imaging. Paracetamol 1 g four times daily was commenced for headache, and oral sodium chloride 1 g three times daily was given with slow sodium correction.

Physiotherapy and occupational therapy assessments on 01/01/2026 identified mild gait instability and impaired fine motor coordination affecting tasks such as fastening buttons and handling utensils. Daily physiotherapy, occupational therapy, and home-safety planning were initiated. Speech and language assessment on 02/01/2026 found an adequate swallow without aspiration and mild word-finding difficulty; no further swallowing or communication intervention was required at that stage.

Repeat CT head on 03/01/2026 showed no progression of the subdural hygroma or new findings, and management was unchanged. Cognition progressively improved, with stable neurological observations and no focal deficits. Mobility and balance improved with therapy; occupational therapy recommended measures including a raised toilet seat, bathroom grab rails, improved lighting, removal of loose rugs, and use of a grabber tool. Social work and community support were involved in discharge planning.

By 05/01/2026, confusion had resolved with GCS 15/15, independent walking, steady gait, and no significant cognitive barriers on occupational therapy assessment. At a subsequent final physiotherapy review on 07/01/2026, he remained neurologically intact, independently managed walking, stairs, and obstacles, and required no further inpatient physiotherapy. He was discharged home clinically stable with home-safety advice and community support arrangements. At discharge, atorvastatin 40 mg daily for seven days and levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily for seven days were documented. Neurology outpatient follow-up was arranged, documented as approximately two weeks to one month, and the GP was informed.

05192757-942f-460d-b4ff-004ec39cc5ee.summary:
- **21/12/2025 – Pre-operative assessment:** Hope Chinwo, 75-year-old woman, was assessed for elective total left hip replacement for severe/end-stage left hip osteoarthritis, with approximately 5 years of progressive pain, stiffness and impaired weight-bearing. Medical history included hypertension and cataract surgery (2018). She used a stick indoors and frame outdoors but was independent with activities of daily living. Examination showed painful, markedly restricted left hip movement without redness or swelling; distal pulses, sensation and overall neurological status were intact. BP was 145/85 mmHg. ECG showed normal sinus rhythm without ischaemic changes. Hb was 11.3 g/dL with otherwise normal blood count, renal function and liver tests.  
- Mild anaemia was treated with **ferrous sulfate 200 mg once daily**; she continued paracetamol 500 mg as required and calcium/vitamin D supplements. No allergies were reported. Anaesthetic assessment found her suitable for spinal anaesthesia. Risks, benefits and recovery expectations were discussed, and written consent was obtained. She was cleared for surgery, with ongoing BP monitoring advised because of hypertension.

- **02/01/2026 – Admission and surgery:** Pre-operative checklist confirmed identity, left-sided surgical site, fasting status, medication reconciliation and no allergies. She was clinically stable and cleared for theatre.  
- Under **spinal anaesthesia**, Dr. Deirdre FitzGerald performed a posterolateral **total left hip replacement** for end-stage osteoarthritis, assisted by Dr. Marcus John Whitehead. Severe degenerative joint changes and significant cartilage loss were found, with no evidence of infection or abnormal surrounding tissue. The left femoral head was removed and a cemented prosthesis implanted. Estimated blood loss was approximately 150 mL, with no intraoperative complications. The femoral head was sent for histological examination.  
- In PACU, observations remained stable (BP 130/85, HR 72, SpO₂ 98% on room air). She was alert, had mild discomfort without significant nausea or vomiting, and the wound was clean and dry. She received IV paracetamol 1 g. Enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneously once daily was commenced for thromboprophylaxis, with early physiotherapy planned.

- **Postoperative course:** Hb fell to 104–105 g/L, assessed as postoperative/peri-operative blood-loss anaemia without need for acute intervention. Ferrous sulfate 200 mg daily was started/continued, with advice regarding hydration, iron-rich diet and repeat Hb monitoring. Pain remained mild and well controlled with paracetamol. The wound remained clean and dry without erythema, discharge, swelling or bleeding; no clinical signs of DVT or infection were documented. Vital signs remained stable.
- Physiotherapy began on the day of surgery. She initially mobilised short distances with a walker while observing hip precautions, including avoiding hip flexion beyond 90 degrees and crossing the legs. She progressed to stair practice and then to crutches with good balance, coordination and adherence to precautions.
- Occupational therapy addressed transfers, dressing and other activities of daily living. She required minimal assistance and was provided with a hip kit. A raised toilet seat and bathroom grab bars were recommended and arranged. Dietary advice included a high-protein diet to support wound healing and recovery.
- By the final physiotherapy assessment, she could ambulate, turn and manage simulated home obstacles safely with crutches and was considered suitable for independent discharge with crutches. Family and GP updates were provided.

- **Discharge planning (05–06/01/2026):** She had minimal pain, was confident with activities of daily living, and was mobilising well with crutches. The plan was discharge home on **06/01/2026** with continued hip precautions, outpatient physiotherapy and clinic follow-up. Planned discharge treatment included paracetamol as required, ferrous sulfate 200 mg daily, and rivaroxaban 10 mg once daily for 7 days for thromboprophylaxis. Wound care, medication use and mobility precautions were explained.

0c04d9fb-d8d0-4ee0-8fc9-0c3f7f148bdf.summary:
Georgina Claire Gurung is a 55-year-old woman with end-stage left hip osteoarthritis, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia and mild osteopenia. Preoperatively, she had a four-year history of progressive left hip pain, stiffness, reduced range of motion and impaired mobility, using a walking stick. Examination showed an antalgic gait, left hip tenderness and restricted movement without erythema or effusion. ECG and urinalysis were normal. Blood tests showed mild anaemia (Hb 10.8 g/dL; subsequently 11.2 g/dL), with normal renal and liver function.

During preoperative assessment in December 2025, no anaesthetic contraindications or allergies were identified. GA combined with spinal block was planned. Ferrous sulfate 200 mg daily was started for anaemia, omeprazole 20 mg daily for two weeks was prescribed due to intermittent ibuprofen use, and GP review of antihypertensive treatment was recommended because of moderately elevated blood pressure. Ibuprofen was to be stopped 48 hours before surgery. Consent was obtained after discussion of operative, anaesthetic and prosthesis-related risks.

She was admitted electively for left total hip replacement. Preoperative examination showed no infection or other contraindication to surgery. She received planned perioperative prophylaxis, including IV cefuroxime and TXA 1 g IV at surgery.

On 03/01/26, she underwent elective left total hip replacement under general anaesthesia and spinal block, performed by Dr Elizabeth Kathryn Singh with Dr Terence John Watson assisting. Severe cartilage erosion and subchondral bone exposure were found; damaged cartilage and bone from the acetabulum and femoral head were removed. A cemented prosthesis with polyethylene acetabular and metal femoral components was inserted. Estimated blood loss was 300 mL, with no complications.

Postoperatively, she remained cardiovascularly and respiratorily stable, with oxygen saturations of 98% on room air and no transfusion required. Initial pain score was 4/10 and improved after IV morphine. Regular paracetamol and PRN tramadol were prescribed; ibuprofen was initially included but later discontinued. She received 24 hours of IV cefuroxime and thromboprophylaxis, initially enoxaparin 40 mg daily, later dalteparin 5000 units subcutaneously until discharge. The wound remained clean and dry without infection, haematoma or significant bleeding, and there were no clinical signs of DVT or other systemic complications.

Physiotherapy began on the day of surgery with bed exercises, ankle pumps and assisted walking using a frame. Over the following days she progressed to partial weight-bearing, gait and balance training, transfers, stair practice and then independent ambulation with crutches. Occupational therapy assessed home safety and recommended a raised toilet seat, bathroom grab rails and a long-handled reacher. By 05/01/26 she was independently performing transfers and activities of daily living, and by 06/01/26 she could mobilise and negotiate stairs independently with crutches.

Postoperative Hb was 10.8 g/dL, regarded as a mild postoperative anaemia, and ferrous sulfate 200 mg daily was continued for four weeks. Pain remained well controlled, the wound was healing without erythema or discharge, and vital signs remained stable. She was discharged with apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily for two weeks, a home exercise programme and follow-up with her GP in six weeks for wound review and outpatient physiotherapy referral.

0f438665-d430-4adb-8acc-c3beed9e4942.summary:
Jack Geoffrey Gray, a 3-year-old boy with no previous medical history and allergies to pollen and macrolides, presented via A&E on 06/01/26 with 24–48 hours of poor oral intake, fewer wet nappies and mild lethargy. He had no vomiting, diarrhoea, rash or respiratory distress. Initial observations were temperature 38.3°C, heart rate 120 bpm and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Examination showed mild dehydration with dry mucous membranes and capillary refill of approximately 2 seconds, mild nasal congestion, and no respiratory or abdominal abnormalities.

He was diagnosed with a viral illness/viral upper respiratory tract infection complicated by mild dehydration and reduced feeding. Paracetamol suspension 120 mg/5 mL, 5 mL, was given for fever. A 10 mL/kg oral normal saline bolus was administered and tolerated well, followed by advice to give ORS in small, frequent amounts. No antibiotics were prescribed. He was admitted to the Paediatric Assessment Unit for observation and supportive care, with IV 0.9% sodium chloride and 5% dextrose at 75% maintenance, monitoring of intake/output and hydration, and PRN paracetamol.

A venous blood gas showed mild metabolic acidosis with pH 7.33 and bicarbonate 17 mmol/L. No other investigations or blood/urine results were documented. Nasal saline drops were started for congestion, with parental education regarding oral rehydration, small frequent feeds, signs of dehydration and nasal care.

Over the following ward reviews, oral intake and hydration improved, with fluids and mashed food tolerated and no further fever documented. IV fluids were reduced to 50% maintenance to encourage oral intake and subsequently discontinued for discharge planning. ENT review found moderate nasal mucosal inflammation consistent with viral URTI, without purulent discharge or anatomical abnormality. Saline nasal drops, saline spray/nasal irrigation and steam inhalation twice daily were advised.

By discharge review, Jack was alert, playful, afebrile and clinically hydrated, with improved eating and drinking and only mild residual nasal congestion. Vital signs were stable, including temperature 36.8°C and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. He was discharged home with advice to continue oral fluids and small meals, use paracetamol as needed, continue saline nasal drops, use saline spray for nasal irrigation and steam inhalation twice daily. Parents were advised to seek medical attention if feeding or hydration worsened, wet nappies reduced or lethargy increased, and to contact his GP if concerned.

136c7916-4f9b-4e5c-bf01-77e9d2c681a2.summary:
Philip Paul Cook, 49-year-old man with hypertension and mild osteoarthritis, presented to the ED on 02/01/2026 after an unwitnessed minor fall at home, followed by progressive confusion and unsteadiness. He denied loss of consciousness, headache, vomiting, visual symptoms, weakness, seizures, chest pain, or shortness of breath. He was alert but disoriented, with GCS 14/15 and no focal neurological deficits; gait was unsteady and required assistance. Initial observations were stable. CT head showed a subdural hygroma without midline shift or acute haemorrhage. Blood tests were largely normal, with mild hyponatraemia documented at sodium 132 mmol/L; dehydration was also noted. He was admitted to the neurology ward for neurological observation.

Initial management included regular neurological observations, IV paracetamol, IV 0.9% sodium chloride for dehydration and hyponatraemia, and neurology review. No surgery or antibiotics were initially required; subsequently, ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily for five days was prescribed prophylactically. Physiotherapy and occupational therapy were commenced for gait instability, balance impairment, and mild fine-motor difficulty. He received mobility, balance, falls-prevention, cognitive, and ADL training, with adaptive equipment including a button hook, long-handled reacher, non-slip mat, shower chair, and walking aids.

During 03–06/01/2026, neurological status remained stable without focal deficits. Confusion and fatigue improved, although mild gait and balance impairment persisted. Sodium remained approximately 132–133 mmol/L. Management progressed from IV fluids to oral hydration advice, sodium chloride supplementation (documented as 600 mg or 1 g three times daily), and fluid restriction to 1.5 L/day. Paracetamol was prescribed as needed for mild headaches or musculoskeletal discomfort. Speech and language assessment identified mild short-term memory and attention difficulties, and cognitive rehabilitation was recommended.

By 07–08/01/2026, he was alert, oriented, and free of headache, dizziness, or confusion. Mobility improved substantially with physiotherapy; he could walk with a stick or rollator, perform transfers, and negotiate stairs independently, with only mild residual unsteadiness. OT and social work completed home-safety and discharge planning. Community care visits and outpatient physiotherapy were arranged, and he was considered safe for discharge on 08/01/2026.

Discharge advice included fall prevention, use of the provided adaptive equipment, and avoidance of anticoagulants unless prescribed. Paracetamol was prescribed as needed for pain/headache, with dosing documented variably as 500 mg 1–2 tablets every 4–6 hours or 1 g four times daily. Follow-up was arranged with neurology in two weeks and the GP within approximately one week; the patient was advised to seek urgent medical attention for severe headache, recurrent confusion, or new neurological symptoms.

137b8481-4f1d-4b7f-babd-20f7117023ad.summary:
Frank Scott Bond, 64-year-old man with hypertension, osteoarthritis and prior TIA (2018), presented on 06/01/26 after a minor fall at home with acute confusion and mild right-sided headache. He reported no loss of consciousness, vomiting, visual symptoms, weakness or speech disturbance. Examination showed mild disorientation with GCS 14/15, but pupils, cranial nerves, power, sensation and coordination were intact. Mild right hip discomfort/bruising and dehydration were noted. Initial BP was approximately 160–165/92–95 mmHg.

CT head on 06/01/26 demonstrated a subdural hygroma without acute intracranial haemorrhage or mass effect. He was admitted to the AMU for conservative management, neurological observations and BP monitoring. Paracetamol 1 g as required was prescribed for headache. Initial urea was 9.8 mmol/L, and mild hyponatraemia was documented with sodium 131 mmol/L. IV 0.9% sodium chloride 1 L over 8 hours, oral hydration and fluid-balance monitoring were commenced, with plans for repeat electrolytes.

During admission, confusion persisted initially without focal neurological deterioration. Occupational therapy noted mild short-term memory and task-sequencing difficulties, and cognitive rehabilitation was recommended. Physiotherapy identified mild unsteadiness; he mobilised with a four-wheeled walker and received balance, coordination and stair-training exercises. Speech and language therapy provided cognitive-linguistic exercises for attention, memory and occasional word-finding difficulty.

Sodium improved to 132–133 mmol/L. Oral electrolyte supplementation with Dioralyte was given, followed by sodium chloride tablets 600 mg twice daily. Headache and confusion gradually improved, with resolution of headache and progressive improvement in orientation. By 08/01/26 he was oriented to person, place and time, although mild fatigue and mobility concerns remained. Home assessment identified bathroom and stair hazards; grab rails were arranged/installed and home-safety education was provided.

By 09–10/01/26, he reported no headache, dizziness or further confusion. Neurological examinations remained stable without focal deficits. Mobility improved to safe independent walking, including stairs, without a walking aid. Speech and language reassessment showed clear speech, normal swallowing and no ongoing significant communication deficit; further SLT was not required. IV fluids were stopped and oral hydration continued.

He was discharged home on 11/01/26 in stable condition, alert and fully oriented, with sodium 133 mmol/L and no focal neurological deficits. Discharge medication was paracetamol 1 g every 6 hours as needed for headache or joint pain. He was advised to maintain oral hydration, follow up with his GP in two weeks, and continue community physiotherapy and home mobility/safety exercises.

1705dd0f-011a-492c-b006-b27e03f2f4ed.summary:
- **22/12/2025 – Preoperative assessment:** Mr Manveer Kumar was assessed for elective total right shoulder replacement for severe, progressive right shoulder pain and stiffness due to end-stage osteoarthritis. Symptoms had worsened over approximately two years, with reduced active and passive range of motion, glenohumeral tenderness, crepitus, and sleep disturbance. He was independent with activities of daily living and mobilised without aids. Medical history included hypertension, acid reflux, and bilateral cataract surgery in 2018. Regular medication was paracetamol 500 mg as required and omeprazole 20 mg daily; no known drug allergies were documented.  
- Preoperative investigations showed mild anaemia with Hb 11.2 g/dL; WCC, platelets, U&E, and LFTs were acceptable. ECG showed sinus rhythm without acute changes and chest X-ray was unremarkable. Ferrous sulfate 200 mg twice daily was commenced, with planned Hb monitoring. Anaesthetic assessment found him clinically stable and fit for general anaesthesia; fasting and hydration instructions were provided. Consent was obtained after discussion of the procedure, risks, expected benefits, recovery, and physiotherapy.

- **03/01/2026 – Admission and surgery:** He was admitted electively in a stable condition for right total shoulder replacement. Examination showed markedly restricted right shoulder movement with crepitus but no deformity, redness, swelling, or infection. Preoperative blood tests and assessments were reviewed, with mild anaemia considered stable and optimised with ferrous sulfate.  
- A total right shoulder replacement was performed under general anaesthesia via an anterior deltopectoral approach for end-stage osteoarthritis. Operative findings were severe glenohumeral degeneration with significant cartilage loss, without infection or periarticular inflammation. Damaged articular cartilage and subchondral bone were removed, and a cemented modular shoulder prosthesis was implanted. Estimated blood loss was minimal and there were no complications.  
- Postoperative treatment included IV cefuroxime 1.5 g every 8 hours for 24 hours, morphine PCA/IV morphine and regular paracetamol for analgesia, shoulder sling immobilisation, wound monitoring, and planned physiotherapy.

- **03/01/2026 – Recovery:** In PACU he regained consciousness and followed commands. Cardiovascular and respiratory status remained stable with oxygen saturation 97% on room air. Pain was treated with IV morphine 2 mg; mild nausea responded to IV ondansetron 4 mg. The wound had no bleeding or haematoma, and he was transferred to Ward B3 in stable condition. Oral morphine 10 mg as required and regular paracetamol 1 g every 6 hours were prescribed.

- **Early postoperative period:** Ward reviews documented mild, manageable pain, stable observations, and a clean, dry wound without erythema, discharge, swelling, or neurovascular compromise. He began mobilisation with physiotherapy and was started on enoxaparin for venous thromboembolism prophylaxis. Physiotherapy included assisted passive and active-assisted range-of-motion exercises, sling education, strengthening, self-care, and safe activities of daily living.

- **Subsequent recovery:** Shoulder mobility improved, pain became minimal or well controlled, and he mobilised short distances with assistance. The wound continued to heal without infection or swelling, with good passive range of motion and no neurovascular compromise. Analgesia was transitioned from IV to oral paracetamol as required; codeine 30 mg every 6 hours as needed was prescribed for breakthrough pain. He was instructed to continue home exercises and sling use.

- **Discharge planning:** By the latest reviews he was comfortable, alert, reporting minimal pain, and had improved shoulder mobility. Final physiotherapy reinforced active range-of-motion and strengthening exercises, posture, sling use, and management of daily activities. He was considered suitable for discharge the following morning if no new issues arose, with oral paracetamol as required for seven days, ongoing home physiotherapy, and orthopaedic outpatient follow-up planned at six weeks.

1dbe23dc-0d1e-431b-81eb-497282b46a14.summary:
Philip Clive Osborne is a 4-year-old boy with a right tibial fracture treated by internal fixation in 2024, mild asthma, eczema, and allergies to penicillin, sulfonamides, pollen, and nuts. He was scheduled for elective removal of the right tibial fixation device. Preoperative assessment on 28/12/25 documented stable asthma with mild wheeze and no acute exacerbation; he was classified ASA II and considered suitable for general anaesthesia. FBC and coagulation tests were performed and subsequently reviewed as satisfactory. Montelukast 4 mg daily was prescribed for two weeks preoperatively, with continued inhalers and two puffs of salbutamol planned before surgery. Consent was obtained from his mother, and avoidance of penicillin- and sulfonamide-based antibiotics was confirmed.

On 07–08/01/26, preoperative reviews found him alert and clinically well, with stable observations, no respiratory distress or active infection, and a well-healed right tibial surgical site without erythema, swelling, tenderness, or instability. Medication reconciliation with his GP found no discrepancies. Planned prophylaxis was IV cefuroxime, with an alternative antibiotic available if required.

On 08/01/26 he underwent removal of the right tibial internal fixation device under general anaesthesia. The device was intact and correctly positioned; surrounding tissue was healthy with no infection or inflammation. The wound was irrigated and closed with sutures and a sterile dressing. Blood loss was minimal (<10 mL), no tissue was removed, and there were no complications.

In recovery he remained haemodynamically and respiratorily stable on room air, became fully awake within 30 minutes, and had no nausea or agitation. Pain was controlled with oral ibuprofen 100 mg. The dressing remained clean and intact without bleeding or discharge. Postoperative plans included paracetamol as needed, and documentation included a 5-day course of cefuroxime suspension; recovery documentation also recorded co-amoxiclav suspension for 5 days.

Postoperative ward reviews documented no pain or breathing difficulty, a clean and healing wound without erythema, swelling, tenderness, warmth, or discharge, and full right lower-limb movement. A mildly elevated CRP of 12 mg/L was noted and monitoring was planned. Cefuroxime IV was planned for 48 hours, with continued analgesia and observation for infection or further CRP elevation.

Physiotherapy and occupational therapy supported weight-bearing, range-of-motion exercises, supervised walking, and use of a paediatric frame/crutch. By 09/01/26 he was independently mobilising along the ward without limp, pain, or discomfort and required no further inpatient physiotherapy. Parents were instructed regarding wound care, infection symptoms, analgesia, crutch use, daily walking, and exercises. Discharge was planned for 09/01/26 with paracetamol and ibuprofen 100 mg liquid three times daily for additional pain relief, GP follow-up, and surgical review in two weeks for suture removal.

28570119-9cdc-4120-98c0-4edb76cf36a3.summary:
Judith Ada Wells, a 39-year-old woman with no documented past medical history, regular medications, or allergies, presented on 07/01/26 with a sudden exertional “thunderclap” headache, described as the worst headache of her life, rated 8/10, with mild nausea. Initial observations were BP 160/90 mmHg and HR 88 bpm. Neurological examinations were repeatedly normal, with no focal deficits, neck stiffness, visual symptoms, or altered consciousness.

CT head at 14:45 showed no intracranial haemorrhage, mass lesion, or other abnormality. Blood tests showed mild leukocytosis (WBC 12.5 × 10⁹/L), mildly elevated CRP (8 mg/L, later 12 mg/L), normal renal and liver function, and subsequently mild hypokalaemia (K⁺ 3.3 mmol/L). The initial impression was reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome (RCVS), and she was admitted under Neurology.

Nimodipine 60 mg orally every 4 hours was commenced, with neurological and blood pressure monitoring. MRI/MRA confirmed RCVS on 08/01/26. Nimodipine was subsequently documented as 30 mg every 4 hours. Oral potassium replacement (KCl 1 g twice daily) was prescribed for hypokalaemia. Mild hyponatraemia (Na 132 mmol/L) was later noted and managed with increased dietary sodium and avoidance of excessive fluid intake. Physiotherapy assessment found mild residual neck stiffness without significant functional impairment; outpatient physiotherapy was planned, with no inpatient sessions required.

Headache severity improved from 7–8/10 initially to 5/10, then 3/10 and 2/10, without development of new neurological symptoms. Blood pressure improved to approximately 125–135/80–85 mmHg and neurological examinations remained normal. Patient education covered RCVS, warning symptoms, lifestyle measures, and avoidance of triggers including intense exertion, stress, triptans, and ergotamines.

Repeat MRA on 11/01/26 showed significant improvement and documented resolution of the cerebral vasoconstriction. By 12/01/26 she reported no further headache, was clinically well with a normal neurological examination, and was discharged home. The discharge plan documented nimodipine 30 mg four times daily, to be tapered over two weeks, with neurology follow-up in four weeks and advice to avoid known triggers. A subsequent GP communication documented discharge medication as amlodipine 5 mg once daily; the notes do not reconcile this difference.

29ea304f-821d-474e-81a1-394ca3945e02.summary:
Ren Suzuki, 40-year-old man with asthma and seasonal allergic rhinitis, allergic to pollen and taking no regular medications, presented to the ED at approximately 01:00 on 05/01/26 with sudden sharp central chest pain (8/10), worse with deep inspiration and movement, associated with mild shortness of breath. Initial observations showed tachycardia and mild tachypnoea (HR 110, RR 24, BP 135/85, SpO₂ 95–96% on room air, temperature 37.1°C). Examination demonstrated mild anterior chest tenderness and subcutaneous crepitus in the neck/chest, with equal air entry and no respiratory distress.

ECG at 02:30 showed sinus tachycardia without ischaemic changes. Chest X-ray at 02:50 demonstrated pneumomediastinum and subcutaneous emphysema, with no pneumothorax documented. He was diagnosed with spontaneous pneumomediastinum, considered likely related to coughing, straining, or increased intrathoracic pressure, without haemodynamic instability. He was admitted to the respiratory HDU for conservative management.

Treatment included paracetamol 1 g four times daily as required/regularly and ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily, with advice to avoid Valsalva manoeuvres, straining, and heavy lifting, and monitoring for respiratory compromise. Omeprazole 20 mg once daily was subsequently started for gastrointestinal protection while taking ibuprofen.

On 05/01/26 he remained clinically stable with mild residual chest pain. Physiotherapy provided diaphragmatic and pursed-lip breathing exercises, education on reducing thoracic strain, and advice to practise breathing exercises every two hours while awake. By 06/01/26 he was comfortable, had no overnight chest pain, and reported improved breathing. Repeat chest X-ray showed a slight reduction in the pneumomediastinum. Analgesia was stopped as he was pain-free, and further imaging was planned.

Subsequent review documented no pain or shortness of breath, stable observations (HR 82, BP 128/78, RR 16, SpO₂ 97% on air), clear chest, and no palpable subcutaneous crepitus. Repeat imaging showed no complications and continued improvement. The final chest X-ray demonstrated complete resolution of the pneumomediastinum and subcutaneous emphysema, with no abnormality; no further imaging was required. Discharge planning was initiated, respiratory outpatient follow-up was arranged, and the patient received education on recurrence symptoms and when to seek urgent medical attention. His GP was updated on 08/01/26.

31f9612b-5a6b-48ea-887b-895772a83b99.summary:
John Michael Gill, a man with hypertension, hyperlipidaemia and previous appendectomy (1998), was assessed in December 2025 for elective right total knee replacement for end-stage osteoarthritis. He had a four-year history of progressive right knee pain and stiffness, worsening over the preceding six months, with intermittent swelling and occasional night pain. Examination showed mild swelling, medial joint-line tenderness and reduced range of motion (0–90°). Pre-operative ECG showed sinus rhythm without acute abnormalities, and FBC, renal and clotting results were acceptable for surgery. Blood pressure was 148/92 mmHg and was optimised with amlodipine 5 mg daily. Ibuprofen was to be stopped one week before surgery and paracetamol 1 g QDS used instead. He had mild anxiety regarding general anaesthesia, with oral midazolam 2 mg planned on the morning of surgery. Consent was completed on 20/12/25, and pre-operative skin preparation with 4% chlorhexidine was advised.

He underwent right total knee replacement for end-stage osteoarthritis under general anaesthesia, using a cemented prosthesis. Significant cartilage erosion and osteophyte formation were found; these were removed and the wound was closed with absorbable sutures and a sterile dressing. Blood loss was minimal and there were no operative complications. Post-operatively, morphine PCA was commenced, cefuroxime 1.5 g IV was prescribed for 24 hours, and he received morphine 2 mg IV for pain and ondansetron 4 mg IV for mild nausea in PACU. He was stable and transferred to the Trauma and Orthopaedics Ward.

Early post-operative review documented pain of 6/10, haemoglobin 110 g/L without need for transfusion, normal urea and electrolytes, and no clinical evidence of infection or DVT. The knee dressing was intact with mild expected swelling and bruising. Enoxaparin 40 mg SC daily was initially prescribed for thromboprophylaxis, later changed to dalteparin 500 units SC daily until discharge. CRP was mildly elevated at 45 mg/L (later recorded as 44 mg/L), with no signs of infection.

Post-operatively, IV cefuroxime and metronidazole were planned for 24 hours, with analgesia and gradual advancement from nil by mouth to clear fluids.
