- **22/12/2025 – Pre-operative assessment:** Yuri Matsumoto, an 8-year-old girl, was assessed for progressive, painless left leg deformity present for approximately one year, with no trauma, swelling, functional limitation, or relevant past medical/family history. Examination showed a well child with full left leg range of motion and no local inflammatory signs. Hb was 10.2 g/dL with other blood results within normal limits; chest X-ray was normal. Oral ferrous sulfate 200 mg once daily was commenced, with repeat Hb planned for 05/01/2026. Anaesthetic assessment cleared her for general anaesthesia with a caudal block. Written consent was obtained from her father after discussion of the procedure, risks, and expected recovery. No known allergies or regular medications were documented.

- **05–06/01/2026 – Admission/pre-operative review:** Repeat Hb was 12.4 g/dL and considered adequate for surgery. She remained clinically well, with no swelling, erythema, tenderness, deformity-related pain, or signs of infection. Blood tests were otherwise within normal limits, apart from a CRP of 12 mg/L, considered likely pre-operative inflammation. She was deemed fit for surgery, with nil by mouth from midnight and planned peri-operative cefazolin.

- **07/01/2026 – Surgery:** Elective left distal femur hemiepiphysiodesis was performed under general anaesthesia with a caudal block for angular deformity/valgus. A guided-growth tension-band device was placed through a lateral distal femur incision. The growth plate appeared healthy, without inflammation, infection, or abnormal tissue. No tissue was removed, blood loss was minimal, and there were no complications. The incision was closed with absorbable sutures and covered with a sterile dressing. Post-operative analgesia included paracetamol and ibuprofen; cefazolin was planned for 24 hours post-operatively.

- **Immediate post-operative recovery:** In PACU she was cardiovascularly and respiratory stable on room air, drowsy but rousable and orientated, with mild operative-site pain rated 3/10. Pain was treated with IV paracetamol. There was no nausea or vomiting, and the wound was clean and dry without bleeding or airway concerns.

- **Post-operative inpatient course:** She reported moderate but manageable pain. The wound remained clean and dry with no erythema, discharge, swelling, or other complications. Oral paracetamol was prescribed as required; a later review documented that antibiotics were not required in the absence of infection. Physiotherapy commenced ankle pumps and assisted knee flexion/extension without significant discomfort. Occupational therapy noted that she could sit and complete seated activities independently but required moderate assistance for standing due to balance difficulty; a lightweight paediatric walking aid was recommended. She subsequently mobilised with crutches under supervision. Hb was 10.8 g/dL, described as mild transient anaemia and clinically insignificant.

- **08/01/2026 – Discharge planning:** Final physiotherapy addressed safe crutch use, weight-bearing support, small steps, posture, and left-leg range-of-motion exercises. She demonstrated confident and safe mobilisation and was discharged with a home exercise programme. Discharge analgesia was paracetamol 250 mg every 6 hours as required and ibuprofen 150 mg every 8 hours with food for 3 days. Outpatient physiotherapy follow-up was advised in 2 weeks, and orthopaedic clinical and radiological review in 6 weeks.

- **01/01/2026 – ED presentation/admission:** Rhys Jenkins, 61-year-old man with COPD, hypertension and hyperlipidaemia, presented with 3 days of worsening shortness of breath, wheeze and chest tightness despite increased salbutamol use. He denied chest pain, fever and haemoptysis. Initial SpO₂ was 89% on room air, with RR 28/min, HR 105 bpm, accessory muscle use and bilateral wheeze. He was started on 2 L/min oxygen via nasal cannula and nebulised salbutamol.
- **Investigations:** ABG showed type 2 respiratory failure with respiratory acidosis (PaCO₂ 7.8 kPa, pH 7.30; later pH 7.28 with PaO₂ 8.5 kPa on oxygen). Chest X-ray showed hyperinflation consistent with COPD exacerbation, without pneumonia or pneumothorax. CRP was elevated, and thick yellow sputum was reported, prompting treatment for suspected bacterial infection.
- **Initial treatment:** Nebulised salbutamol and ipratropium every 4 hours, oxygen targeting SpO₂ 88–92%, and prednisolone 30 mg daily for 7 days were commenced. Antibiotic plans included amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily; IV co-amoxiclav was also documented during the ward review. He was admitted under Respiratory Medicine.
- **01/01/2026 – Respiratory support and therapy:** He remained fatigued with wheeze and accessory muscle use but maintained SpO₂ around 91% on 2 L/min oxygen. Respiratory physiotherapy commenced, including diaphragmatic breathing exercises. His next of kin was updated.
- **02/01/2026 – Early improvement:** Repeat ABG showed reduced CO₂ and improved pH with partial resolution of respiratory acidosis. Oxygen weaning was initiated. He remained mildly fatigued with reduced wheeze and was receiving 4 L/min oxygen with SpO₂ 92% during one review. CRP was reported as falling, and doxycycline was prescribed in subsequent plans to complete antibiotic treatment. Physiotherapy taught active cycle of breathing techniques, postural drainage and controlled breathing. Occupational therapy assessed home function and recommended a perching stool, bathroom grab rails and community OT follow-up.
- **03/01/2026 – Clinical progress:** Shortness of breath and wheeze continued to improve. He was stable on 1 L/min oxygen with SpO₂ 94%, RR 18/min and improved breath sounds; CRP had decreased to 18 mg/L. He could ambulate without significant dyspnoea. Respiratory physiotherapy progressed to strengthening, balance and corridor walking. Dietetics recommended a high-protein diet and Ensure twice daily. Smoking cessation education, inhaler education and referral to smoking cessation services were provided. Discharge planning began.
- **04/01/2026 – Functional improvement:** He tolerated ambulation with a walking frame and breathing exercises, with only mild exertional dyspnoea. Occupational therapy found him functionally independent or requiring minimal assistance, safe with a walking aid, and suitable for home discharge. Influenza and pneumococcal vaccines were administered. Nebulised therapy improved his breathing and wheeze. Later review showed SpO₂ 96% on room air, clear chest examination and CRP 8 mg/L, indicating resolution of inflammation. Prednisolone was stopped in one plan, and doxycycline was prescribed.
- **05/01/2026 – Discharge:** He was alert, comfortable, independently mobile and free of shortness of breath, with RR 16/min, SpO₂ 96% on room air and no wheeze or respiratory distress. Final oxygen-weaning trial was successful, and no further supplemental oxygen was required. He received discharge education on salbutamol and tiotropium inhaler technique, medication adherence, recognising early exacerbation symptoms and emergency contacts. Respiratory clinic follow-up was arranged for 2 weeks, with pulmonary rehabilitation encouraged and smoking cessation referral made. Discharge antibiotic and steroid instructions were documented as doxycycline 100 mg daily for 5 days and prednisolone 30 mg daily for 2 further days; separate discharge education also advised amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily for 5 days.
